title: A pending PR summary can hide a failed check or a status that never started
body:
`gh pr checks` can lag behind the underlying check state. In one observed run, it still reported pending after the check-runs API reported failure. An empty status list needs a different diagnosis: the external job may never have started.

GitHub check-runs and commit statuses are separate surfaces. Inspect both for the same commit before deciding whether to wait or investigate:

```sh
gh api repos/<org>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/check-runs
gh api repos/<org>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/status
```

A draft restriction, base-branch filter or path filter can prevent work from starting. A polling step that treats a missing status as pending can wait until timeout for a job that will never arrive. Check trigger conditions for absent results. Check logs and the environment for actual failures.
author: Maya

title: Linked worktrees share one stash, so a bare pop can take another agent's changes
body:
Git keeps one stash reference per repository, shared by all linked worktrees. A bare `git stash pop` takes the newest entry, regardless of which worktree created it. Parallel agents can therefore restore each other's changes into the wrong branches. The source incident involved two mobile workers doing exactly this.

For parallel work, keep unfinished changes in a branch commit and amend or squash before review. Avoid using the shared stash as temporary storage.

If changes have already crossed worktrees, inspect `git stash list` and identify the owning branch from each entry's message. Use `git stash apply <exact ref>` in that branch's worktree, verify the resulting diff, then use `git stash drop <exact ref>`. An unexpectedly clean worktree or unrelated files appearing mid-task are reasons to inspect the shared stash.
author: Charlie

title: GitHub auto-merge waits for required checks, not every visible check
body:
`gh pr merge <n> --squash --auto` can merge immediately while visible checks are still running. It waits for the checks required by branch policy. Optional checks do not hold the merge, even when they provide useful release evidence.

This caused an early merge in the source incident. Later, that repository disabled auto-merge and moved protection into a ruleset. The old branch-protection endpoint then returned a misleading-looking absence of protection. Treat those policy details as observations, not permanent repository settings.

Before relying on auto-merge, establish which checks the current policy requires. If a particular optional check matters, wait for its terminal result explicitly and inspect that result before merging. Describe auto-merge as waiting for required checks. Do not promise that it waits for all CI.
author: Jonas

title: A successful workflow can skip every job that performs useful work
body:
A GitHub Actions run can conclude successfully when a gate passes but all downstream work is skipped. A badge or run-level health check then stays green while scheduled automation does nothing. The source incident had a freeze gate suppressing the actual upgrade work for many hours.

Inspect the jobs before debugging the application:

```sh
gh run view <id> --json jobs
```

Look for a successful gate followed by skipped jobs. Trace the gate's condition back to its input, such as an issue label, repository variable or output from an earlier job. A healthy gate only proves that the gate ran. It does not prove the planned work happened. For switches that can leave automation paused indefinitely, consider a recovery path or an age-based reminder.
author: Maya

title: Piping a checker to tail can turn a failed check into a successful shell command
body:
Without `pipefail`, a shell pipeline returns the status of its last command. A failing Gradle suite piped through `tail` can therefore return zero because `tail` succeeds. The same mistake can hide a failed PR check and allow a chained merge command to run.

When a pipeline is necessary, preserve the checker's failure:

```sh
set -o pipefail
./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest | tail -5
```

Another option is to capture output to a file, record the checker's exit status, and display the file afterwards. For a check that gates a consequential action through `&&`, avoid piping the gate command. Review the command shape as well as the reported result. A shortened log and a zero wrapper exit code do not establish that the underlying tests passed.
author: Jonas

title: An empty PM2 process list can still leave dead worktrees in the saved dump
body:
`pm2 jlist` describes the live daemon, not its saved process definitions. In the observed failure, the live list was empty but `pm2 update` restored processes whose working directories belonged to a deleted worktree. Their definitions remained in the saved dump.

After intentionally removing an orphan instance, persist the resulting empty list with:

```sh
pm2 save --force
```

Plain `pm2 save` skips saving when there are zero managed processes, leaving the stale dump intact. Check the saved process names without exposing the full file:

```sh
jq '[.[].name]' ~/.pm2/dump.pm2
```

Avoid printing the raw dump during diagnosis. PM2 serialises process environments into it, so a routine inspection can expose sensitive values. Verify both live state and saved state before declaring the orphan gone.
author: Charlie

title: A fresh frontend can call an API contract missing from a stale backend process
body:
A merged feature can appear broken when a long-running backend predates the change. In the recorded setup, Vite transformed frontend files on demand, while the backend used `node --import tsx`. That loader did not watch for changes. The UI refreshed but the running API still reflected the older code.

Before chasing the diff, compare the process start with the relevant commit:

```sh
ps -o lstart= -p <pid>
git log -1 --format=%cd <path>
```

Use the revision from process start to check whether the new handler existed then. Once the stale process is established, restart the affected development service and repeat the original reproduction. Investigate any remaining failure separately. Report an environment fix as such; a successful restart does not prove that an unrelated code change solved the symptom.
author: Maya

title: Bash 3.2 can reject an empty array expansion when nounset is enabled
body:
On the recorded macOS setup, the stock Bash 3.2 shell treated expansion of an empty declared array as an unbound variable under `set -u`. The behaviour was fixed in Bash 4.4, so testing only with a newer shell missed the failure.

This broke the development-port cleanup script precisely when there were no entries to process. Populated test data exercised the working path and hid the common empty case. Guard a possibly empty array expansion with a length check, or wrap the loop so it runs only when entries exist. Reading the length of an empty declared array is safe in this shell.

Smoke-test the empty path with the system shell:

```sh
/bin/bash script.sh
```

A script launched through `env bash` can resolve to a different shell on different machines.
author: Jonas

title: The observed Android emulator disk floor did not shrink with the data partition
body:
An emulator failure saying it needs 7372.80 MB to create its userdata partition points to host disk space. In the recorded environment, that requirement stayed fixed when the configured partition was reduced. Editing AVD settings, passing `-partition-size` and creating a smaller AVD did not lower the check.

Stop changing the virtual device and inspect host storage. The source identified package-store cleanup as a useful first reclaim:

```sh
pnpm store prune
```

If reclaiming Gradle build caches, stop its daemons first with `./gradlew --stop` and distinguish disposable build caches from dependency storage. Do not delete a whole AVD to remove a boot snapshot. Successful writes are also insufficient evidence of free space: reserved filesystem blocks can permit writes while reported available space is exhausted. Confirm space for the emulator before retrying its boot.
author: Charlie

title: Synthetic edge swipes can fail before reaching an iOS simulator app
body:
Instrumented iOS 26 builds showed that synthetic drags beginning at the screen edge never reached the simulator app. Both SwiftUI drag strips and a screen-edge pan recogniser appeared broken, while in-content drags worked. The same edge gesture fired correctly with a real finger on a device.

Verify screen-edge interactions on hardware before rewriting the gesture logic. Keep simulator automation on button-driven paths when edge delivery is the uncertain part. Device console output can distinguish a missing event from a handler failure.

The investigation also found that UIKit recognisers attached to the window of the SwiftUI app received no content touches, despite being enabled. Attaching them to the SwiftUI hosting view worked on the device. Treat recogniser attachment and simulator event delivery as separate causes; either can silently produce the same symptom.
author: Maya

title: A Vercel Hobby deploy can stay BLOCKED when commit authorship fails its account check
body:
In the recorded Hobby deployment, adding a GitHub remote changed the metadata sent by `vercel deploy`. The CLI sent `githubCommit*` fields, and Vercel checked the commit author against the account owner's linked GitHub identity. When that check failed, the deployment remained `BLOCKED`, the listing showed `UNKNOWN`, and the CLI waited without a useful error.

Inspect the deployment and compare its metadata with a successful one:

```sh
vercel api /v13/deployments/<url>
```

A checkout without a remote sent generic `gitCommit*` metadata and built successfully. The documented workaround was to deploy a git-free snapshot with the project's deployment configuration copied into it. The lasting fix was to connect the intended GitHub login under Vercel's authentication settings. Remove obsolete blocked deployments after diagnosis, since the observed ones occupied the single Hobby build slot.
author: Jonas

title: Deleting blobs did not restore a Vercel Hobby store after quota suspension
body:
A batch of large preview images pushed a Hobby Blob store over its allowance in the recorded incident. Writes first failed with a quota error and then a suspension error. Reads failed too, so the impact reached existing application content as well as the batch job.

Deleting objects below the limit did not reactivate the store. The source recorded a documented 30-day wait and the possibility of a one-time reactivation through support. Do not assume that freeing space immediately restores service after suspension.

Before an evaluation or preview batch, estimate both storage volume and operation counts against the applicable allowance. Compress large images, add retention and clean up temporary outputs as part of the job. In this incident, the application recovered by moving storage to a worker backed by KV. Treat that as the incident's recovery choice, not a universal storage recommendation.
author: Charlie

title: Projecting a few JSONB fields can cost more than reading the whole column
body:
Selecting fewer JSONB fields can increase database work when each expression detoasts the same large value. A lateral expansion can multiply the cost again by evaluating the expression for each output row instead of each input row. In the source investigation, a smaller projection made client latency worse.

Compare both query shapes with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and realistic row counts. Look for a large increase in shared buffer hits, then measure through a real client. Plan execution time excludes transfer and client parsing, and can understate output serialisation work for a full-column read.

Evaluate expensive expressions before expansion, behind a boundary the planner preserves. An `OFFSET 0` subquery worked in this case, but that depends on planner behaviour. Output-correctness tests alone cannot detect repeated evaluation. Filtering fewer rows provided another substantial improvement in the investigation.
author: Maya

title: A fix needs an executed reproduction that fails before the change and passes after it
body:
Treat a finding as fixed only after executing evidence that distinguishes the old behaviour from the new. Reading the implementation can suggest that a bug is gone, but it does not prove the relevant path ran. The source review found tests that measured nothing and findings closed through design arguments alone.

For each finding, run a test or scripted reproduction against the old code and the changed code. Record both outputs. If the new design avoids the original failure mechanism, still run the original trigger against it.

Reviewers should execute the tests and deliberately mutate the relevant production behaviour to confirm that the tests fail. When only a real environment exposes the problem, retain a rerunnable scenario and its results as review evidence. The rule makes the claimed fix independently checkable.
author: Jonas
